A2.text:
Aysel is twenty-two. She lives in Baku with her grandmother, Firuza. Firuza has a small bakery in the Old City. She makes shekerbura and pakhlava every morning, and she has done it for forty years.

One evening, Aysel filmed her grandmother. Firuza's hands moved very fast, and she sang an old song. Aysel put the short video online and went to bed.

In the morning, her phone did not stop. The video was viral. It had two million views. The algorithm showed it to people in Turkey, Germany and even Brazil. Every post in Aysel's feed was about the bakery.

The next day, there was a long line outside the shop. A famous influencer came with a camera. Other bakeries wanted to jump on the bandwagon and made the same videos.

Not all comments were nice. Some trolls wrote that the cakes were not clean. Aysel was angry. She read the comments all night and did not sleep. She had to block ten people.

On Sunday, Aysel looked at her screen time: nine hours a day. Her grandmother laughed. “The cakes are the same,” Firuza said. “Put the phone down and help me.”

Aysel put the phone in a drawer and made shekerbura with her grandmother.

questions.why: “Firuza has a small bakery in the Old City.”

questions.q: How many views did the video have in the morning?

questions.why: “Some trolls wrote that the cakes were not clean.”

questions.q: Other bakeries wanted to “jump on the bandwagon”. What does this mean?
questions.why: They copied the idea: they “made the same videos”.

questions.q: What did Firuza want Aysel to do?
options: Put the phone down and help her
questions.why: “Put the phone down and help me.”

B1.text:
When Aysel filmed her grandmother making shekerbura, she wasn't trying to become famous. Firuza has run a tiny bakery in Baku's Old City for forty years, and Aysel simply wanted to keep a memory of her quick hands and the old song she always sings while she works. She posted the forty-second clip before bed and forgot about it.

By morning, the video had gone viral. Two million people had watched it, and the engagement was unbelievable: thousands of likes, comments in a dozen languages, people sharing it with their mothers. Somehow the algorithm had decided that the whole world needed to see a grandmother folding pastry, and suddenly every post in Aysel's feed seemed to be about the bakery.

For a few weeks, the little shop was in the spotlight. Tourists queued down the street. A well-known influencer arrived with a ring light and asked Firuza to dance for the camera. Other cafés decided to jump on the bandwagon and filmed their own grandmothers, real or not.

Then the trolls found them. One account said the kitchen was dirty; another said the video was fake. The comments seemed written to stir up anger, and they worked. Aysel spent her nights replying, arguing and deciding who to block. Her screen time reached nine hours a day, and she started checking her phone even while she was serving customers.

It was Firuza who noticed. One evening she gently took the phone out of Aysel's hand and put a rolling pin in it instead.

“The dough doesn't care how many people are watching,” she said. “It only cares if you're paying attention.”

Aysel turned off her notifications that night. The bakery is still busy, but now she posts one video a month — and she reads the comments only on Sundays.

questions.q: Why did Aysel first film her grandmother?
options: To keep a memory of her
questions.why: She “simply wanted to keep a memory of her quick hands and the old song”.

questions.q: What made the video reach people all over the world?
questions.why: “The algorithm had decided that the whole world needed to see” it.

questions.q: What did some other cafés do?
options: They copied the idea with their own videos
questions.why: They “decided to jump on the bandwagon and filmed their own grandmothers”.

questions.q: The influencer paid Firuza for the video.
questions.why: The text says the influencer asked her to dance, but nothing about money.

questions.q: The trolls wanted to “stir up anger”. What does “stir up” mean here?
questions.why: Their comments were written to make people angry — “and they worked”.

questions.q: What does Firuza mean by “It only cares if you're paying attention”?
options: Baking needs your full focus, not your phone
questions.why: She takes the phone away and gives Aysel a rolling pin: the work needs her attention.

B2.text:
Aysel had never thought of her grandmother as content. Firuza had been running the same narrow bakery in Baku's Old City for forty years, getting up at five to fold shekerbura while humming songs nobody under sixty recognised. So when Aysel filmed her one evening, it was out of tenderness rather than ambition — a forty-second clip she expected a handful of cousins to watch.

By breakfast it had gone viral. Two million views, and a level of engagement that people in marketing spend whole careers chasing: tens of thousands of comments, many from strangers who said the video had reminded them of their own grandmothers. Whatever the algorithm saw in those floury hands, it pushed them into feeds from Istanbul to São Paulo.

Being in the spotlight turned out to be strangely exhausting. Tourists queued past the mosque on the corner. An influencer with three million followers turned up uninvited, rearranged the pastries for better lighting and asked Firuza to wink at the camera. Within a week, half the cafés in the neighbourhood had decided to jump on the bandwagon, posting suspiciously similar clips of suspiciously young grandmothers.

Then came the backlash. A handful of trolls — some of them, Aysel suspected, owners of rival bakeries — accused Firuza of using frozen dough, posted blurry photos of a kitchen that wasn't hers and seemed determined to stir up as much outrage as possible. Aysel took every comment personally. She replied at two in the morning, argued with people who had no faces and spent entire evenings deciding whom to block. When her phone reported an average screen time of nine hours a day, she assumed it was a mistake.

Firuza was less surprised. One night she simply took the phone, set it face down on the counter and handed Aysel a rolling pin.

“Two million people watched me for forty seconds,” she said. “The dough needs you for forty minutes. Which one is real?”

Aysel still posts, but now it's once a month and she reads the comments only on Sundays. The queues are shorter, yet the regulars are back. And sometimes, rolling out pastry before dawn, she catches herself humming one of those songs nobody under sixty is supposed to know.

words.phrase: out of tenderness rather than ambition

questions.q: Why did Aysel make the first video?
options: Out of love for her grandmother
questions.why: “It was out of tenderness rather than ambition.”

questions.q: What did the influencer do at the bakery?
options: Moved the pastries for better light and asked Firuza to wink
questions.why: She “rearranged the pastries for better lighting and asked Firuza to wink at the camera”.

questions.q: Who did Aysel suspect some of the trolls were?
questions.why: “Some of them, Aysel suspected, owners of rival bakeries.”

questions.q: Firuza was shocked by Aysel's screen time.
Being “in the spotlight” was exhausting. What does “in the spotlight” mean?
options: On a stage in a theatre
Getting a lot of public attention
questions.why: Tourists queued and an influencer came: everyone was watching the bakery.

questions.q: What is Firuza's point when she compares forty seconds with forty minutes?
options: Real work and real people matter more than online attention
Aysel should film the whole process
questions.why: Strangers watch for seconds; the work in front of you needs real time — “Which one is real?”
